newsitem.title: USA: Ribozyme, Chiron gene therapy advances.
newsitem.headline: Ribozyme, Chiron gene therapy advances.

text.p: Ribozyme Pharmaceuticals Inc and Chiron Corp said Thursday that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved an Investigational New Drug Application that will allow a gene therapy approach using ribozymes against HIV to be tested in a Phase I/IIa clinical trial.
This FDA action follows approval of the proposed study by the Recombinant DNA Advisory Committee of the NIH in April, 1996.
Also seeking approval was the City of Hope National Medical Center and Childrens Hospital Los Angeles.

The physician-sponsored clinical trial will be carried out at City of Hope as part of a collaboration among RPI, Chiron, City of Hope and Childrens Hospital. The product has several important components, including the use of multiple ribozymes to avoid development of resistance to therapy.

In addition, by inserting the ribozyme construct into "stem cells" (CD34+ cells), it may be possible to rebuild portions of the immune system. This construct protected cells over their lifetime in preclinical studies, and has also demonstrated substantial protection against both laboratory strains of HIV and a clinical isolate compared to controls.

"Initiating this clinical trial achieves several important milestones for RPI and its ribozyme technology platform," said Ralph Christoffersen, president and CEO of RPI. "This is the first time ribozymes will be applied to human stem cells, and is RPI's first IND. In addition, it also incorporates from Chiron both their GMP retroviral manufacturing expertise and proprietary retroviral cell lines that have an outstanding safety record. Indeed, it is exciting to see the first RPI example of the translation of the ribozyme technology from a concept into a clinical reality."

The clinical trial, which will begin in the first half of 1997, will utilize a retroviral construct manufactured by Chiron Technologies Center for Gene Therapy to transduce CD34+ cells ex vivo from five HIV positive patients. These transduced cells will then be reinserted into the patients. Clinical end points to be monitored during the study include general safety, level of bone marrow engraftment and survival of ribozyme-containing cells.

The first successful inhibition of HIV by a ribozyme was published by a research team at City of Hope in 1990. This group also developed and tested the double ribozyme approach to be used in this clinical trial. Investigators at CHLA were the first to accomplish retroviral delivery of these genes into human hematopoietic stem cells.

The development of hammerhead ribozymes for HIV treatment was initially supported by the National Institutes of Health, in a program called the National Cooperative Drug Discovery Groups for AIDS. This program initially supported collaborative efforts of the City of Hope, CHLA and RPI. The current translation of this work is supported in part by the NIH through their Strategic Program for Innovative Research in AIDS Treatment, a grant awarded to the City of Hope and CHLA and in part by funds from City of Hope, RPI and Chiron.
